messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 49
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Architect
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 52

Mark, a 49-year-old architect of North American descent, has been struggling with the aftermath of witnessing a traumatic event. He lives in a quiet suburban neighborhood with his wife, Sarah, who is supportive but notices changes in Mark's behavior that worry her deeply. The trauma occurred about two years ago when Mark was working on an architectural project at a busy downtown office building. One morning, while he was reviewing blueprints, there was a sudden commotion outside. He looked up to see a man being brutally attacked by several individuals. Despite his efforts to alert security and call for help, the attackers fled before authorities could arrive. Mark witnessed the aftermath of the assault, feeling helpless as emergency personnel worked to revive the victim. Since that day, Mark has experienced a range of distressing symptoms. He often finds himself reliving the event through vivid flashbacks, particularly when he hears sirens or sees crowded public places. These flashbacks are so intense and realistic that they disrupt his work, causing him to lose focus on architectural designs and detailed plans. The trauma has also led to significant avoidance behaviors. Mark now avoids downtown areas and any location where large crowds gather, such as concerts or sports events. He feels a constant sense of unease, as if danger lurks around every corner, which makes even walking through his neighborhood feel risky. Mark’s sleep is frequently disrupted by nightmares. In these dreams, he often finds himself powerless to stop the attack, reliving the helplessness and fear he felt that day. These nightmares leave him exhausted and anxious, affecting his ability to function effectively at work and spend quality time with Sarah. Recently, Mark has noticed an increase in irritability and anger outbursts. Small inconveniences or misunderstandings can trigger intense frustration and impatience. His wife observes this change and worries that their once close relationship is becoming strained under the pressure of his emotional volatility. His job as an architect requires a high level of concentration, creativity, and attention to detail—qualities that have been significantly compromised by his PTSD symptoms. He often feels detached from his work and colleagues, finding it hard to engage in collaborative projects or brainstorming sessions without being distracted by intrusive thoughts about the attack he witnessed. The physical symptoms of hyperarousal are also noticeable. Mark frequently experiences a racing heart rate, sweating, and heightened startle responses when exposed to sudden noises or movements. These reactions can be particularly distressing during team meetings or presentations where unexpected questions might trigger his anxiety. Mark has become increasingly isolated over time. He used to enjoy weekend hiking trips with Sarah but now finds excuses to avoid these activities, fearing that being in nature could expose him to more unseen dangers. This isolation further strains their relationship, as Sarah struggles to understand why Mark withdraws emotionally and physically from the activities they once shared. Despite his efforts to push through each day, Mark’s PTSD continues to impact every aspect of his life—his work performance, relationships, and overall well-being. He remains haunted by what he witnessed that fateful morning, longing for a way to reclaim control over his life without feeling constantly on edge or haunted by the memory of the attack. Mark’s journey is one of ongoing struggle and resilience, as he continues to navigate through the challenges posed by PTSD, searching for ways to find peace and reconnect with the world around him.
